title: Maximin Relative Improvement: Fair Learning as a Bargaining Problem
claim: Absolute-scale robust criteria pick lopsided solutions across groups, while a scale-invariant relative measure equalizes gains between groups.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared x-axis, vertical dashed lines marking each solution
description: Two side-by-side line plots share a hyperparameter β on the x-axis. The left panel plots per-group risk R_g(β) for White (blue) and Non-White (red) groups. Dotted horizontal baselines mark each group's baseline risk, and shaded regions show the potential improvement. The right panel plots the same curves rescaled as relative improvement ρ_g(β): the red group rises roughly linearly and the blue group falls steeply below zero. Two vertical dashed lines mark the two solutions. Purple is the minimax-regret solution β_MMR = 0.144, and green is the maximin-relative-improvement solution β_MMRI = 0.128. Dots on the curves are annotated with percentages. Purple shows 82% and -74%, and green shows an equal 57% for both groups. Legends are in each panel. The eye goes first to the curve crossing at the green dot.
caption: Left: per-group risk Rg(β). Right: relative improvement ρg(β), where minimax regret yields (−74%, 82%) while maximin relative improvement achieves (57%, 57%).
abstract: When deploying a single predictor across multiple subpopulations, we propose a fundamentally different approach: interpreting group fairness as a bargaining problem among subpopulations. This game-theoretic perspective reveals that existing robust optimization methods such as minimizing worst-group loss or regret correspond to classical bargaining solutions and embody different fairness principles. We propose relative improvement, the ratio of actual risk reduction to potential reduction from a baseline predictor, which recovers the Kalai-Smorodinsky solution. Unlike absolute-scale methods that may not be comparable when groups have different potential predictability, relative improvement provides axiomatic justification including scale invariance and individual monotonicity. We establish finite-sample convergence guarantees under mild conditions.
